entries.name: An exception beats the general rule it contradicts

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Exceptions Supersede General Rules / p. 5

entries.evidence: General rules govern each part of the game. For example, the combat rules tell you that melee attacks use Strength and ranged attacks use Dexterity. The game also includes elements—class features, feats, weapon properties, spells, magic items, monster abilities, and the like—that sometimes contradict a general rule. When an exception and a general rule disagree, the exception wins.
entries.note: The precedence rule of the whole corpus, and the reason no mapped rule here can be read alone: every general rule in this map is defeasible by an element outside it. A test must show that where two rules the engine holds disagree and one is an exception, the exception's answer is returned, and that the engine can say which rule it applied. The corpus names the classes of element that carry exceptions -- class features, feats, weapon properties, spells, magic items, monster abilities -- and every one is outside this slice, so what the engine can hold today is the rule, not its instances.

entries.name: A D20 Test succeeds when the total equals or exceeds the target number

entries.evidence: A saving throw—also called a save—represents an attempt to evade or resist a threat, such as a fiery explosion, a blast of poisonous gas, or a spell trying to invade your mind. entries.evidence: The game uses actions to govern how much you can do at one time. You can take only one action at a time. entries.evidence: Various class features, spells, and other abilities let you take an additional action on your turn called a Bonus Action. You can take only one Bonus Action on your turn, so you must choose which Bonus Action to use if you have more than one available. You choose when to take a Bonus Action during your turn unless the Bonus Action’s timing is specified. Anything that deprives you of your ability to take actions also prevents you from taking a Bonus Action.

entries.evidence: Certain special abilities, spells, and situations allow you to take a special action called a Reaction. The Opportunity Attack, described later in “Playing the Game,” is the most common type of Reaction. When you take a Reaction, you can’t take another one until the start of your next turn. If the reaction interrupts another creature’s turn, that creature can continue its turn right after the Reaction. In terms of timing, a Reaction takes place immediately after its trigger unless the Reaction’s description says otherwise.

The interruption rule matters as much -- the interrupted creature continues its turn after the Reaction, so a Reaction does not end a turn.

In those situations, it’s time for social interaction, which takes many forms. For example, you might try to convince a burglar to confess to wrongdoing or try to flatter a guard. The Game Master assumes the roles of any nonplayer characters who are participating.
entries.note: Declined as framing. The passage says what a social interaction is and who plays the NPCs, and demands nothing of an engine. The two rules inside this section that do -- the NPC's attitude and the two ways an interaction progresses -- are mapped separately. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: An NPC's attitude is Friendly, Indifferent or Hostile

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Social Interaction / p. 10

crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent; the three attitudes are defined there, and trial 8 maps only its conditions.

entries.evidence: An NPC’s attitude toward your character is Friendly, Indifferent, or Hostile, as defined in “Rules Glossary.” Friendly NPCs are predisposed to help, and Hostile ones are inclined to hinder.
entries.note: A closed three-value vocabulary, which is why it is in scope where the section around it is not: an engine can hold an attitude and the Influence action can alter it. What each attitude does is defined outside the slice, so the engine holds the value and not its effect -- the same shape as a condition it has not been given the definition of.

entries.name: A social interaction progresses through roleplaying and ability checks

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Social Interaction / p. 10

entries.evidence: Social interactions progress in two ways: through roleplaying and ability checks.
entries.note: One sentence, and it is the sentence that bounds what an engine may be asked: exactly one of the two ways is computable, and the other is the table's. An engine that answered a social interaction without being told a check was called for would be answering the roleplaying half, which it cannot.

entries.name: Roleplaying, and how the GM has an NPC react

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Roleplaying / p. 10

entries.evidence: Roleplaying is, literally, the act of playing out a role. In this case, it’s you as a player determining how your character thinks, acts, and talks. Roleplaying is part of every aspect of the game, and it comes to the fore during social interactions. As you roleplay, consider whether you prefer an active approach or a descriptive approach. The GM uses an NPC’s personality and your character’s actions and attitudes to determine how an {11} NPC reacts. A cowardly bandit might buckle under threats of imprisonment. A stubborn merchant refuses to help if the characters badger her. A vain dragon laps up flattery. When interacting with an NPC, pay attention to the GM’s portrayal of the NPC’s personality. You might be able to learn an NPC’s goals and then use that information to influence the NPC. If you offer NPCs something they want or play on their sympathies, fears, or goals, you can form friendships, ward off violence, or learn a key piece of information. On the other hand, if you insult a proud warrior or speak ill of a noble’s allies, your efforts to convince or deceive will likely fail.
entries.note: Declined as advice, and the clearest case in the slice: a cowardly bandit buckling under threats and a vain dragon lapping up flattery are guidance to a person about a judgement the corpus gives that person. Recorded because it is a section, not a sentence, and a reader finding two pages unmapped needs to know they were read. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: When dice decide a social interaction

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Social Interaction / Ability Checks / p. 11

crossReferences.cites: the GM will typically ask you to take the Influence action

entries.evidence: Ability checks can be key in determining the outcome of a social interaction. Your roleplaying efforts can alter an NPC’s attitude, but there might still be an element of chance if the GM wants dice to play a role in determining an NPC’s response to you. In such situations, the GM will typically ask you to take the Influence action.
entries.note: Declined, and the distinction is worth stating: the Influence action itself is in scope as a row of `actions-table`, and this passage is about when a GM reaches for it -- 'if the GM wants dice to play a role', 'typically'. Nothing here an engine applies. The advice that follows about leading with a proficient character is the same. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: What the exploration rules cover

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Exploration / p. 11

entries.evidence: Exploration involves delving into places that are dangerous and full of mystery. The rules in this section detail some of the ways adventurers interact with the environment in such places.
entries.note: Declined as a section opener: it names what follows and states nothing. Recorded so that the walk over p. 11 is accounted for unit by unit. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: Equipment helps on an adventure

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Adventuring Equipment / p. 11

crossReferences.cites: See “Equipment” for rules on many items
crossReferences.unmapped: Equipment (pp. 83-102) is outside this map's extent, which ends at p. 12; the items' rules are stated there.

entries.evidence: As adventurers explore, their equipment can help them in many ways. For example, they can reach out-of-the-way places with a Ladder, perceive things they wouldn’t otherwise notice with a Torch or another light source, bypass locked doors and containers with Thieves’ Tools, and create obstacles for pursuers with Caltrops. See “Equipment” for rules on many items that are useful on adventures. The items in the“Tools” and “Adventuring Gear” sections are especially useful. The weapons in “Equipment” can also be used for more than battle; you could use a Quarterstaff, for example, to push a sinister-looking button that you’re reluctant to touch.
entries.note: Declined as advice. A Ladder reaching a high place and a Quarterstaff pushing a button are suggestions, and every rule the passage gestures at is in Equipment, outside the slice. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: Sight affects some tasks, and what obscures it hinders them

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Vision and Light / p. 11

entries.evidence: Some adventuring tasks—such as noticing danger, hitting an enemy, and targeting certain spells—are affected by sight, so effects that obscure vision can hinder you, as explained below.
entries.note: The premise the three rules below it rest on, and worth its own entry because it names which tasks sight reaches: noticing, attacking, and targeting certain spells. An engine that applied an obscurement to every roll would be wrong, and this sentence is where the scope of the effect is stated.

entries.name: A Lightly Obscured area gives Disadvantage on sight-based Perception checks

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Obscured Areas / p. 11

entries.evidence: An area might be Lightly or Heavily Obscured. In a Lightly Obscured area—such as an area with Dim Light, patchy fog, or moderate foliage—you have Disadvantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sight.
entries.note: Narrow on purpose, and a test must hold it there: Wisdom (Perception) checks that rely on sight, and nothing else. A Perception check by hearing is unaffected, and so is every other check and every attack roll -- which `heavily-obscured` below is not.

entries.name: A Heavily Obscured area gives the Blinded condition to anyone trying to see in it

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Obscured Areas / p. 11

crossReferences.unmapped: The Blinded condition is defined in the Rules Glossary (p. 179), outside this map's extent and inside trial 8's slice, which maps it as `blinded`. Nothing in the contract joins a pointer to an entry in another map of the same corpus -- #433's third hypothesis.

entries.evidence: A Heavily Obscured area—such as an area with Darkness, heavy fog, or dense foliage—is opaque. You have the Blinded condition (see “Rules Glossary”) when trying to see something there.
entries.note: The sharpest instance of the composition question this trial was chosen for. The rule is complete only with the Blinded condition, that condition is mapped -- by trial 8, in another map, over the same pinned corpus -- and the pointer can only be recorded as unmapped, because `resolvedBy` holds an id in this map. The engine an this slice would produce knows a creature is Blinded and not what that means.

entries.name: Bright Light, Dim Light and Darkness

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Light / p. 11

entries.evidence: The presence or absence of light determines the category of illumination in an area, as defined below. Bright Light. Bright Light lets most creatures see normally. Even gloomy days provide Bright Light, as do torches, lanterns, fires, and other sources of illumination within a specific radius. Dim Light. Dim Light, also called shadows, creates a Lightly Obscured area. An area of Dim Light is usually a boundary between Bright Light and surrounding Darkness. The soft light of twilight and dawn also counts as Dim Light. A full moon might bathe the land in Dim Light. Darkness. Darkness creates a Heavily Obscured area. Characters face Darkness outdoors at night (even most moonlit nights), within the confines of an unlit dungeon, or in an area of magical Darkness.
entries.note: Three categories in one passage, and one entry because the rule is the partition: each category is defined by what it does to the area, and two of the three do it by naming an obscurement -- Dim Light creates a Lightly Obscured area, Darkness a Heavily Obscured one. Bright Light creates neither, which is what makes it the third value and not the absence of a value. A test must assert all three and the two links.

entries.name: The four special senses this corpus defines

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Special Senses / p. 11

crossReferences.cites: “Rules Glossary” defines the following special senses
crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent; Blindsight, Darkvision, Tremorsense and Truesight are defined there, and trial 8 maps only its conditions.

entries.evidence: Some creatures have special senses that help them perceive things in certain situations. “Rules Glossary” defines the following special senses: Blindsight Darkvision Tremorsense Truesight
entries.note: A closed list of four names whose meanings are all outside the slice -- the same shape as `npc-attitude`, and mapped for the same reason: an engine can hold which senses a creature has, and a reader must be able to see that the list is four and not more. What each sense does, this slice cannot say.

entries.name: Hiding is the Hide action, and the GM decides when it is possible

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Hiding / p. 11

entries.evidence: Adventurers and monsters often hide, whether to spy on one another, sneak past a guardian, or set an ambush. The Game Master decides when circumstances are appropriate for hiding. When you try to hide, you take the Hide action.
entries.note: Two halves with different owners: whether circumstances allow hiding is the GM's, and what hiding then is -- the Hide action, a Dexterity (Stealth) check by `actions-table` -- is the engine's. An assertion because the gate arrives from a person; the engine demands it and resolves the check it is then owed.

entries.name: Interacting with an object is usually resolved by description

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Interacting with Objects / p. 11

entries.evidence: Interacting with objects is often simple to resolve. The player tells the GM that their character is doing something, such as moving a lever or opening {12} a door, and the GM describes what happens. Sometimes, however, rules govern what you can do with an object, as detailed in the following sections.
entries.note: The default, and it is a rule about when the rules apply: most object interactions have no mechanics at all, and the four sections that follow are the exceptions. An engine's honest answer to 'what happens when I move a lever' is that the corpus does not say, and this entry is why that is an answer rather than a gap.

entries.name: What an object is for the purpose of the rules

locator.citation: Playing the Game / What Is an Object? / p. 12

entries.evidence: For the purpose of the rules, an object is a discrete, inanimate item like a window, door, sword, book, table, chair, or stone. It isn’t a building or a vehicle, which are composed of many objects.
entries.note: A definition with an explicit exclusion, and the exclusion is the load-bearing half: a building and a vehicle are not objects, so no object rule reaches them. A test must refuse to break a building with `breaking-objects`.

entries.name: One free object interaction per turn when time is short

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Time-Limited Object Interactions / p. 12

crossReferences.cites: as explained in “Combat” later in “Playing the Game.”
crossReferences.unmapped: Combat (pp. 13-16) is outside this map's extent and is trial 7's slice, which maps the same limit from the turn's side.

entries.evidence: When time is short, such as in combat, interactions with objects are limited: one free interaction per turn. That interaction must occur during a creature’s movement or action. Any additional interactions require the Utilize action, as explained in “Combat” later in “Playing the Game.”
entries.note: Three rules: one free interaction per turn, it must fall inside the creature's movement or action, and further interactions cost the Utilize action. 'When time is short, such as in combat' is the corpus gating a rule on a state it does not define -- combat is an instance and not the condition -- and an engine outside combat has no way to know whether the limit applies. Recorded here; the gate the corpus does state is trial 7's turn.

entries.name: Searching finds a hidden object only where the search is described

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Finding Hidden Objects / p. 12

entries.evidence: When your character searches for hidden things, such as a secret door or a trap, the GM typically asks you to make a Wisdom (Perception) check, provided you describe the character searching in the hidden object’s vicinity. On a success, you find the object, other important details, or both. If you describe your character searching nowhere near a hidden object, a Wisdom (Perception) check won’t reveal the object, no matter the check’s total.
entries.note: The second sentence is the rule an engine must hold, and it is a refusal: a search described nowhere near the object fails whatever the total, so the check is gated on a fact no roll can overcome. A test must show a natural 20 failing to find an object the search was not near.

entries.name: Gear is carried without weight rules unless the GM invokes carrying capacity

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Carrying Objects / p. 12

crossReferences.cites: the rules for carrying capacity in “Rules Glossary.”
crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent; carrying capacity is defined there, and trial 8 maps only its conditions.

entries.evidence: You can usually carry your gear and treasure without worrying about the weight of those objects. If you try to haul an unusually heavy object or a massive number of lighter objects, the GM might require you to abide by the rules for carrying capacity in “Rules Glossary.”
entries.note: A rule whose default is 'no rule': weight is ignored until a person decides it is not. The engine holds no encumbrance unless told to, and the rules it would then apply are outside the slice, so being told is as far as it can get.

entries.name: A fragile nonmagical object breaks automatically as an action

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Breaking Objects / p. 12

crossReferences.cites: the rules on breaking objects in “Rules Glossary.”
crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent; the rules on breaking objects are stated there.

entries.evidence: As an action, you can automatically break or otherwise destroy a fragile, nonmagical object, such as a glass container or a piece of paper. If you try to damage something more resilient, the GM might use the rules on breaking objects in “Rules Glossary.”
entries.note: Automatic, with no check and no damage roll, and bounded by three conditions the engine can test: fragile, nonmagical, and an action spent. Anything more resilient leaves the slice. 'Fragile' is exemplified and not defined -- a glass container, a piece of paper -- and that is the corpus's own limit, carried as it is.

entries.name: Establishing a marching order

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Marching Order / p. 12

entries.evidence: The adventurers should establish a marching order while they travel, whether indoors or outdoors. A marching order makes it easier to determine which characters are affected by traps, which ones can spot hidden enemies, and which ones are the closest to those enemies if a fight breaks out. You can change your marching order outside combat and record the order any way you like: write it down, for example, or arrange miniatures to show it.
entries.note: Declined as advice. 'Should establish' and 'record the order any way you like' bind nothing, and the uses the passage gives -- who a trap affects, who spots an enemy -- are left to the GM with no rule attached. OutsideCurrentScope.

entries.name: The five hazards this corpus defines

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Hazards / p. 12

crossReferences.unmapped: The Rules Glossary (pp. 176-191) is outside this map's extent; Burning, Dehydration, Falling, Malnutrition and Suffocation are defined there. Trial 8's slice covers those pages and maps the conditions rather than the hazards, so four of the five are unmapped by any map of this corpus.

entries.evidence: Monsters are the main perils characters face, but other dangers await. “Rules Glossary” defines the following hazards: Burning Dehydration Falling Malnutrition Suffocation

extraction.renderedReading: p. 12 prints the five hazard names in two columns beneath the sentence -- Burning and Dehydration in the first, Falling and Malnutrition in the second, Suffocation below them -- and the extraction reads them across, giving Burning Dehydration then Falling Malnutrition then Suffocation.

entries.note: A closed list of five whose meanings are all outside the slice, like `special-senses` and `npc-attitude`. Mapped so that a reader can see the list is five: an engine told a creature is Burning holds a hazard it cannot resolve, and knows that it cannot.

entries.name: The GM may summarise travel or use the travel pace rules

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Travel / p. 12

crossReferences.cites: see the movement rules in “Combat” later in “Playing the Game.”
crossReferences.unmapped: Combat (pp. 13-16) is outside this map's extent and is trial 7's slice, which maps movement.

entries.evidence: During an adventure, the characters might travel long distances on trips that could take hours or days. The GM can summarize this travel without calculating exact distances or travel times, or the GM might have you use the travel pace rules below. If you need to know how fast you can move when every second matters, see the movement rules in “Combat” later in “Playing the Game.”
entries.note: Whether the travel rules apply at all is a person's decision, so it is an assertion and not a gate: there is no rule in the corpus that makes travel pace reachable, only a GM who elects it. An engine asked for a journey's duration must be told that the pace rules are in use.

entries.name: A group travels at a Fast, Normal or Slow pace, and mounts double it for an hour

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Travel Pace / p. 12

crossReferences.cites: (see “Equipment” for a selection of mounts for sale)
crossReferences.unmapped: Equipment (pp. 83-102) is outside this map's extent, which ends at p. 12.

crossReferences.cites: “Gameplay Toolbox” has rules that affect which pace you can choose
crossReferences.unmapped: The Gameplay Toolbox (pp. 192-253) is outside this map's extent and is mapped by no trial; the terrain rules that restrict a pace are stated there.

crossReferences.cites: as shown on the Travel Pace table

entries.evidence: While traveling outside combat, a group can move at a Fast, Normal, or Slow pace, as shown on the Travel Pace table. The table states how far the party can move in a period of time; if riding horses or other mounts, the group can move twice that distance for 1 hour, after which the mounts need a Short or Long Rest before they can move at that increased pace again (see “Equipment” for a selection of mounts for sale). “Gameplay Toolbox” has rules that affect which pace you can choose in certain types of terrain.
entries.note: The mount rule is the harder half and is quoted with the rest because it is one sentence: twice the distance for one hour, then a Short or Long Rest before that again. Both rests are defined outside the slice, so an engine can compute the doubled hour and cannot tell when the mounts are ready again. A test must show the doubling and the refusal.

entries.name: How far each pace travels per minute, hour and day

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Travel Pace / p. 12

entries.evidence: Pace Minute Hour Day Fast 400 feet 4 miles 30 miles Normal 300 feet 3 miles 24 miles Slow 200 feet 2 miles 18 miles

extraction.renderedReading: p. 12 prints the Travel Pace table under a spanning header 'Distance Traveled Per …' with columns Pace, Minute, Hour and Day, and three rows: Fast 400 feet / 4 miles / 30 miles, Normal 300 feet / 3 miles / 24 miles, Slow 200 feet / 2 miles / 18 miles. The extraction runs each row's four cells together.

entries.note: A finite table, so the whole of it is quoted and never a sample: three paces times three periods, and a test must assert all nine distances. The day figures are not the hour figures multiplied by anything the corpus states -- 4 miles an hour gives 30 miles a day, not 32 or 96 -- so the engine reads the table and derives nothing.

entries.name: What each pace does to Perception, Survival and Stealth checks

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Travel Pace / p. 12

entries.evidence: Each travel pace has a game effect, as defined below. Fast. Traveling at a Fast pace imposes Disadvantage on a traveler’s Wisdom (Perception or Survival) and Dexterity (Stealth) checks. Normal. Traveling at a Normal pace imposes Disadvantage on Dexterity (Stealth) checks. Slow. Traveling at a Slow pace grants Advantage on Wisdom (Perception or Survival) checks.
entries.note: Three rules in one passage because they partition one choice, and the asymmetry is the point: Fast imposes Disadvantage on three kinds of check, Normal on one, Slow grants Advantage on two and imposes nothing. A test must assert all three rows and that Normal leaves Perception and Survival alone.

entries.name: A land vehicle chooses a pace; a waterborne vessel's speed replaces one

locator.citation: Playing the Game / Vehicles / p. 12

crossReferences.unmapped: Equipment (pp. 83-102) is outside this map's extent; the vehicles and their speeds are listed there.

entries.evidence: Travelers in wagons, carriages, or other land vehicles choose a pace as normal. Characters in a waterborne vessel are limited to the speed of the vessel, and they don’t choose a travel pace. Depending on the vessel and the size of the crew, ships might be able to travel for up to 24 hours per day. “Equipment” includes vehicles for sale.
entries.note: The rule that switches the pace model off: in a waterborne vessel there is no pace, so `travel-pace-effects` has nothing to apply and the vessel's speed governs. A test must show a character on a ship with no pace and no Stealth penalty. 'Up to 24 hours per day' depends on the vessel and the crew, both outside the slice.
